input: When a binary mixture is held at a fixed pressure and allowed to come to equilibrium, it will generally organise itself into two phases, and the question that naturally arises is what condition has to be satisfied for this two-phase state to count as a genuine equilibrium. The fundamental condition, which is usually regarded as the cornerstone of the whole subject, is that the chemical potential of each component must be the same in both phases. In other words, for the system to be truly at equilibrium, there must be no net tendency for either component to move from one phase into the other, and it is the equality of the chemical potentials that captures this requirement in a precise mathematical form. This is, of course, a statement about the state towards which the system moves, rather than about the speed with which it gets there. If the chemical potential of a component were higher in one phase than in the other, then that component would tend to transfer across the boundary between the phases, and the transfer would carry on until the difference had been eliminated. It is also worth emphasising that the two phases do not have the same composition at equilibrium: each phase has its own composition, and these compositions are determined by the equilibrium condition itself, while the overall composition of the mixture as a whole determines simply how much of each phase happens to be present. No numerical data are needed in order to understand this picture, since the ideas involved are essentially conceptual in nature and apply to binary mixtures quite generally, whatever the particular components of the mixture happen to be and whatever the fixed pressure at which the system is held may be.
target: A binary mixture at fixed pressure reaches phase equilibrium when its two phases coexist with no net transfer of either component between them. The equilibrium condition is equality of chemical potential across the phases. For each component, the chemical potential in one phase equals the chemical potential in the other; transfer is driven by a difference in chemical potential, and a component moves from the phase in which its chemical potential is higher to the phase in which it is lower until the difference is gone. The condition is stated in words first because it governs everything that follows: any equation for the equilibrium compositions is a way of writing this equality for a particular mixture, and the equality is the requirement the equation has to satisfy. Temperature is uniform across the phases and the fixed pressure is common to both, so chemical potential is the only driving force left to balance. Composition is not balanced. Each phase keeps its own composition, set by the equality of chemical potentials, and the two equilibrium compositions differ because the phases are different environments for the two components: one phase favours the component that concentrates there. The overall composition of the mixture decides the amounts of the phases, not their compositions. A mixture rich in one component holds more of the phase in which that component concentrates, and a mixture whose overall composition falls outside the interval between the two equilibrium compositions cannot split at all: it exists as a single phase, because no pair of phases can meet the equality and the overall balance together. The same statement covers a mixture already in two phases that is disturbed: change the temperature and the compositions move, transfer resumes, and the phases settle again only where the chemical potentials are once more equal in each component.
